 Best 2kWh Portable Power Stations in 2026: Jackery vs. Anker vs. EcoFlow vs. BLUETTI
 The 2kWh portable power station has become something of a sweet spot for home backup. It is large enough to run a refrigerator, networking equipment, lights, electronics and plenty of other essentials for a meaningful amount of time, but still small enough that one person can theoretically move it without requesting assistance from a forklift.
 The problem is that the specifications make many of these batteries look nearly interchangeable. Jackery offers 2,042Wh. Anker and EcoFlow both offer 2,048Wh. BLUETTI gives you 2,073.6Wh.
 That difference is almost meaningless in real use.
 What matters much more is that one weighs 39.5 pounds while another weighs more than 53 pounds. One accepts 400W of solar while two others accept 1,000W. One delivers 3,000W of AC power while another tops out at 2,200W. Some can add expansion batteries and others cannot.
 Those are the differences I would use to choose among them.
 After comparing the current 2kWh models, my overall pick is the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 . The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is the one I would choose if weight matters most. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus is considerably more capable if you need high AC output or expect to expand your system later. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 has strong specifications but needs to win on price because it is the heaviest of this group and cannot be expanded.
 Disclosure: Gadget Wisdom may earn a commission from qualifying purchases made through Amazon links on this page. I have not personally load-tested all four of these power stations. This comparison is based on current manufacturer specifications, features and the ways I think they make sense for actual backup-power use.

 All four use lithium iron phosphate, or LiFePO4/LFP, battery chemistry. That is what I would want in a power station I expected to keep for years and maintain as emergency equipment rather than something I planned to replace after a few hundred charge cycles.
 Best Overall: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2
 The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 strikes the best balance in this group.
 It stores 2,048Wh, delivers up to 2,400W of normal AC output and handles a 4,000W peak. Yet it weighs only 41.7 pounds, barely more than the Jackery and considerably less than either the EcoFlow or BLUETTI.
 More importantly, Anker did not get the weight down by turning it into a stripped-down battery box. It accepts up to 800W of solar input, provides two high-power USB-C ports capable of up to 140W each, includes a TT-30 outlet and can be expanded with an Anker SOLIX BP2000 Gen 2 battery to roughly 4kWh.
 That combination gives it room to grow beyond basic refrigerator-and-router duty without making you carry a 50-plus-pound unit from day one.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 on Amazon 
 Anker also rates the C2000 Gen 2 for a 10ms UPS switchover. I would still use a traditional UPS for sensitive networking equipment and a NAS rather than replacing one with a giant power station merely because the spec sheet says UPS. But it is useful when the C2000 is sitting between the wall and equipment you want to keep running through an outage.
 The C2000 Gen 2’s biggest limitation relative to the EcoFlow is output. A 2,400W inverter is enough for a huge range of household equipment, but the EcoFlow’s 3,000W inverter gives it noticeably more headroom for high-draw appliances.
 For most people shopping in this size range, though, I think the Anker offers the best compromise.
 Best If You Actually Want to Carry It: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is the lightweight champion here, although calling a 39.5-pound battery lightweight requires some generosity with the English language.
 Still, the difference is substantial. It is almost 14 pounds lighter than the BLUETTI while storing essentially the same amount of energy.
 The Jackery provides 2,042Wh of capacity, 2,200W of continuous AC output and a rated 4,400W surge. It has three AC outlets, USB-C output up to 100W and uses an LFP battery rated by Jackery for 4,000 cycles to at least 70% capacity.
 Check the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 on Amazon 
 There is a tradeoff. The Explorer 2000 v2 accepts a maximum of 400W of solar input. That is half what the Anker accepts and less than half the 1,000W maximum of the EcoFlow and BLUETTI.
 For an overnight outage, that may mean very little. For several days without grid power, it matters quite a bit.
 Suppose you have consumed 1,500Wh overnight and wake up to a sunny morning. A theoretical 1,000W solar array has a much better chance of replacing a large portion of that energy during the useful daylight window than a system limited to 400W. Real solar output will of course be lower than the panels’ nameplate rating much of the time because of clouds, sun angle, temperature and other losses.
 The Jackery therefore makes the most sense to me for someone who wants a self-contained 2kWh battery, expects to recharge primarily from the wall and values portability more than building a larger solar-backed system.
 Most Capable: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus
 The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus is the brute-force option.
 Its battery is still 2,048Wh, virtually identical to the Anker, but EcoFlow pairs it with a 3,000W AC inverter and rates surge output at 6,000W. It also accepts up to 1,000W of photovoltaic input.
 That 3,000W output changes what you can realistically attempt.
 A refrigerator barely notices whether your power station can supply 2,200W or 3,000W. Neither does a router, television or laptop. But high-draw kitchen appliances, power tools, pumps and other larger loads can bring a smaller inverter much closer to its limit.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus on Amazon 
 EcoFlow also gives this model considerably more room to grow. The company supports configurations from the original 2kWh battery up to approximately 10kWh using compatible extra batteries and the appropriate expansion hardware.
 At that point you are moving well beyond the idea of a portable battery sitting next to a refrigerator. You are beginning to assemble a meaningful home-backup system.
 The price you pay for all of that capability is not merely financial. The DELTA 3 Max Plus weighs roughly 48.7 pounds. That is manageable, but it is nine pounds heavier than the Jackery. If you expect the battery to live in one part of the house most of the time, I would not care much. If you expect to carry it up basement stairs regularly, I would care quite a lot.
 EcoFlow rates the unit for less than 10ms UPS switching and provides four standard 120V AC outlets along with USB and high-current DC outputs. It is the machine I would choose from this group if inverter capability and future expansion mattered more than minimum weight.
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2: Strong Hardware, but Watch the Price
 The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 is an interesting machine because several of its headline specifications are excellent.
 It has the largest battery here at 2,073.6Wh, although the difference from 2,048Wh is too small to matter. More importantly, it delivers 2,600W of AC output and accepts as much as 1,000W of solar input.
 Those are serious specifications for outage use.
 Check the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 on Amazon 
 BLUETTI also gives it app control and UPS capability, with a stated switchover within 15ms. Its 1,000W photovoltaic input is particularly attractive if you expect solar charging to be an important part of your backup plan.
 Then we get to the compromises.
 The Elite 200 V2 weighs 53.4 pounds, making it the heaviest of these four. It is also not directly expandable with BLUETTI’s B80, B230 or B300-series expansion batteries. If you eventually decide that 2kWh is not enough, you cannot simply bolt another battery onto the Elite 200 V2 in the way you can expand the Anker or EcoFlow systems.
 That makes the purchase price particularly important.
 Portable power stations are discounted so frequently that I would never rank them purely by MSRP. A $300 sale can change the answer. If the BLUETTI is substantially cheaper than the Anker or EcoFlow when you buy, 2,600W of output and 1,000W of solar input can make it an excellent deal. At similar pricing, I prefer the flexibility of the other two.
 Why 2,042Wh vs. 2,074Wh Barely Matters
 It is very easy to stare at battery-capacity numbers because they provide a nice clean way to rank products.
 In this group, don’t bother.
 The smallest battery is 2,042Wh and the largest is 2,073.6Wh. The difference is only 31.6Wh, or about 1.5%.
 A 100W load would theoretically consume that difference in less than 20 minutes, before accounting for inverter losses and other real-world variables. Differences in efficiency, standby consumption and operating conditions can easily matter as much or more.
 For practical shopping purposes, these are all 2kWh batteries.
 How Long Will a 2kWh Power Station Run a Refrigerator?
 This is one of the most useful applications for a battery in this class, and also one of the hardest to answer with a single number.
 A refrigerator does not normally consume its rated wattage continuously. The compressor cycles on and off, and consumption varies substantially by refrigerator size, age, room temperature, how frequently the doors are opened and whether the appliance is recovering after having been without power.
 If your refrigerator averages 70W over time, a 2,000Wh battery contains enough theoretical energy for roughly 28 hours. At 100W average consumption, the theoretical number falls to around 20 hours.
 You will get less than the simple division suggests because the battery and inverter are not 100% efficient and because you generally do not want to build an emergency plan that assumes every last watt-hour will be available.
 A reasonable way to think about a 2kWh station is that it can often keep an efficient refrigerator operating through an overnight outage while simultaneously handling smaller loads such as networking equipment, phones and some lighting. Actual runtime needs to be measured with your refrigerator rather than taken from somebody else’s marketing chart.
 Output Watts and Battery Watt-Hours Are Different Things
 This causes endless confusion in power-station shopping.
 Watt-hours tell you roughly how much energy the battery stores. Watts tell you how much power the inverter can deliver at one moment.
 The EcoFlow does not run a 100W refrigerator 36% longer than the Jackery merely because its inverter is rated at 3,000W instead of 2,200W. Their batteries are almost the same size.
 The EcoFlow’s larger inverter instead means it can support a heavier collection of simultaneous loads or an individual appliance that demands more power.
 Think of battery capacity as the size of the fuel tank and inverter output as the width of the pipe coming out of it.
 Do You Actually Need 3,000W of Output?
 Probably not if your outage plan consists of a refrigerator, freezer, modem, router, television, laptops, phones and lights.
 Those are relatively modest loads. A 2,200W Jackery already provides plenty of headroom for most combinations of them.
 The higher-output EcoFlow becomes more compelling when you begin adding devices such as microwaves, kettles, coffee makers, induction burners, larger pumps and power tools.
 There is an important catch: a 2kWh battery is still only a 2kWh battery.
 Running a 1,500W space heater from one of these stations may be technically possible. It is also an excellent method for turning a large expensive battery into an empty large expensive battery in a little over an hour.
 High inverter output gives you the ability to run demanding equipment. It does not create more stored energy.
 Solar Input Matters More During a Multi-Day Outage
 For the first few hours without electricity, solar charging barely enters my decision. I want the battery charged before the storm and ready to go.
 Day two is different.
 The Jackery’s 400W maximum solar input is perfectly useful, but the 800W Anker and 1,000W EcoFlow and BLUETTI systems have a much higher ceiling for replenishing a depleted 2kWh battery during limited daylight.
 Do not interpret a 1,000W solar-input specification as a promise that you will actually harvest 1,000W all afternoon. Portable panels live in the real world, where clouds exist, sunlight arrives at imperfect angles and trees have an irritating habit of being located exactly where you need the sun.
 But a higher input ceiling gives you more opportunity to harvest available sunlight when conditions are good.
 This is also where our backup-power strategy begins to extend beyond simply buying a battery. A power station can get you through an outage. A power station with enough generation behind it begins to become a repeatable energy system.
 Expansion Changes the Long-Term Value
 I would think carefully about whether 2kWh is all you will ever want.
 The Anker C2000 Gen 2 can be paired with an expansion battery to reach roughly 4kWh. EcoFlow goes substantially further, supporting DELTA 3 Max Plus configurations up to about 10kWh with compatible expansion batteries and hardware.
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 and BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 are much more self-contained propositions.
 There is nothing inherently wrong with that. If you want a portable 2kWh box, buying an elaborate expandable ecosystem you will never expand accomplishes very little.
 But if this purchase is the first step toward backing up more of the house, expansion becomes one of the most important differences in the table.
 What I Would Buy for Different Uses
 For General Home Backup: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2
 This is my favorite balance. It is relatively light, has plenty of inverter output, accepts 800W of solar and leaves you an upgrade path to around 4kWh.
 For Moving Between the House, Car and Campsite: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2
 Saving nine or fourteen pounds matters more once you actually start carrying these things. If 2,200W is enough and you do not need a large solar array or expansion battery, the Jackery’s portability is a meaningful advantage.
 For Higher-Demand Appliances or a Growing Backup System: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus
 The 3,000W inverter, 1,000W solar input and expansion path up to approximately 10kWh make this the most capable platform in the group. You pay for that capability in weight and, depending on current pricing, potentially money.
 For a Good Sale: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2
 This may sound faintly complimentary, but it is not meant that way. Power stations are a category where pricing moves dramatically. The Elite 200 V2 gives you 2,600W output and 1,000W solar input. If a promotion puts it materially below the expandable competitors, the value equation can become very favorable very quickly.
 Should You Buy a 2kWh Battery or a Generator?
 If you have not yet decided that a battery is the right answer, I would not start by choosing among these four.
 A battery power station is quiet, can run safely indoors, starts instantly and needs virtually no attention while operating. A combustion generator can keep producing electricity for days as long as you can safely operate it outdoors and keep supplying fuel.
 Those are fundamentally different advantages.
 We have a full comparison in our guide to portable power stations vs. generators for power outages .
 A hybrid system can also make sense: use a battery overnight for quiet indoor power, then use a generator for larger daytime loads and to replenish the battery. We will be digging further into that approach as we expand our home backup-power coverage.
 My Ranking
 If all four cost approximately the same amount, this is how I would rank them:
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 — best overall balance of weight, output, charging and expansion.
 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus — best capability, especially if 3,000W output or major expansion matters.
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 — best portable choice and arguably the better buy than either of the first two for someone who will never need expansion or heavy loads.
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 — excellent output and solar capability, but its weight and lack of expansion make price particularly important.
 I would not treat that ranking as permanent. Check actual prices before buying. If one of these is $400 cheaper than the others during a sale, that is a real specification too.
 The Bigger Question: What Are You Trying to Keep Running?
 Buying a 2kWh power station because 2kWh sounds substantial is backwards.
 Make a list first. Refrigerator. Freezer. Internet. NAS. CPAP. Furnace blower. Sump pump. Television. Lights. Microwave. Whatever actually matters in your house.
 Then look at both starting power and energy consumption.
 That exercise may tell you that a 1kWh battery is plenty. It may tell you that even 2kWh is nowhere near enough. It may also tell you that the best solution is not a larger battery but a generator, solar panels, an expansion battery or some combination of them.
 That is where I want to take this series next. The useful question is no longer simply whether portable power stations work. They do. The useful question is how much backup power your particular house actually needs—and how to build it without buying thousands of dollars of battery that sits unused in a corner.

 How many watt-hours do you actually need?
Start from the load, not the product page. Add up what each device draws and how many hours a
 day it genuinely runs, and you will usually land somewhere between 400 and 900 watt-hours a day.
 A 45 quart compressor fridge is the anchor: it draws roughly 30 to 45 amp-hours a day at 90F
 ambient, which is 400 to 550 watt-hours once you multiply by nominal voltage. Lights add 100 to
 200 watt-hours. A laptop is 50 to 60 watt-hours per charge, and phones are noise by comparison.
To convert a station's rating into the amp-hour language the rest of a 12V build speaks, divide
 watt-hours by 12.8 , the nominal voltage of a LiFePO4 pack. The
 Delta 3 Plus at 1024Wh is therefore roughly 80Ah , which is very close
 to what a 100Ah lithium house battery actually gives you at a sensible depth of discharge. That
 equivalence is the single most useful number on this page, because it lets you compare a sealed
 station against a DIY bank without arguing about marketing units.
Then apply the rule that saves people from buying twice: size for the days you will not charge,
 not the days you will. If you drive every day and have a roof array, one kilowatt-hour is
 generous. If your pattern is to park at a trailhead on a Friday and not move until Sunday
 afternoon, in trees, you need double. Work your own figure with the
 power consumption calculator before you
 read another spec sheet.

 Which portable power station should most overlanders buy?
The Bluetti Elite 200 V2 at under $1,000. The case is

 charge, and a 1kWh unit gives you about two fridge days while the Elite gives you
4.1. It does that at about 50 percent less per watt-hour than the
1,024Wh Delta 3 Plus at under $1,000, so

 class here, and the maker rates the cells to 4,000 cycles.
It also accepts up to 1,000W of solar input, and that number matters more
 than it looks. A station that caps solar at 200W can never quite keep up with a fridge plus
 incidentals on a cloudy day, so you slowly drain over a week. With a high ceiling, two
 Renogy 200W panels plus a portable return
 more than a full day of load on a clear day by the arithmetic further down this page. Match the
 array to the input ceiling with the
 solar array calculator rather than buying
 panels the station cannot use.
The price of all that is weight. At 53.6 lb it is more than twice the
23.8 lb Jackery, and it is a unit you strap down and leave in the vehicle
 rather than one you carry to a picnic table. If that is a deal breaker, the honest 1kWh

under $500, the lightest 1kWh LiFePO4 unit here, and the
 Bluetti AC180 at under $500, which has the most
 capacity of the 1kWh class, a well regarded UPS mode and the lowest cost per watt-hour on this page. Pick the Jackery if the station moves between
 vehicle and camp, the AC180 if it lives in a cabinet and never moves again.
The EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus is still a sound unit,

 default, because the same money now buys twice the capacity on day one.
 What does the beginner tier actually get you?
The entry tier here is not a compromised version of the middle tier, it is a different length of
 trip. The EcoFlow River 3 Max Plus at under $500
holds 858 watt-hours, which is roughly 67 amp-hours, and that runs a small fridge for a long
 weekend without the anxious battery check at 6am. It will not run a hair dryer, a microwave or
 an induction burner, because its inverter tops out at 990W.
The Anker SOLIX C1000 at under $500 is the
 best capacity per dollar in the entry tier: a full kilowatt-hour with an 1800W inverter at
about 10 percent less per watt-hour than the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2. Its 58 minute AC recharge sounds like marketing until
 your only charging window is a two hour drive between camps and a coffee stop with an outlet.
 The reason it is not the overall pick is capacity: 2.1 fridge days against
4.1, and it does not expand, so the capacity you buy is the capacity you own
 forever.
Both entry units share the one limitation nobody mentions in the listings: the 12V car input.
 Most vehicle sockets are fused at 10 to 15A, which caps charging near 120 to 180 watts, so
 refilling a 1kWh station from the cigarette lighter takes the better part of a driving day. If
 you plan to lean on driving to charge, budget for a wired 12V input at 8A or better and treat
 the socket as a trickle rather than a charging strategy.
 How do you recharge one in a vehicle without waiting all day?
There are three inputs and they are not equal. Wall power is fastest and irrelevant off-grid.
 Solar is the one that makes a station a real off-grid system. The 12V vehicle socket is the one
 everybody tries first and the one that disappoints.
For solar, the useful arithmetic is: daily watt-hours equals panel watts multiplied by peak sun
 hours multiplied by a system derate of 0.75 for a flat
 roof-mounted array through an MPPT controller. A 200W panel at 5 peak sun hours therefore
 returns roughly 750Wh , which is about 59 amp-hours at 12.8V.
 That is one fridge day plus a little, from one panel, on a good day. Two panels turn a station
 into something that does not go backwards.
A portable panel you aim at the sun outproduces the same wattage lying flat on a roof by a wide
 margin, and it is the only option if you camp in trees. The
 EcoFlow 220W bifacial portable panel at
under $500 plugs into an EcoFlow station without an adapter hunt, which sounds trivial and is the
 single most common source of a returned solar order. A fixed roof array trades that peak output
 for never having to set anything out, which is the right trade if you move camp daily.
 How much of the pack does a fridge really take?
More than the sticker suggests and less than people fear. A compressor fridge does not draw
 continuously, it cycles. The published draw is what the compressor takes while running, and the
 number that empties a battery is that figure multiplied by duty cycle, which is driven almost
 entirely by ambient temperature and insulation quality.
In practical terms, a well insulated 45 litre unit like the
 ICECO VL45 at under $1,000 sits nearer 30 amp-hours a
 day in mild weather and climbs toward 45 in desert heat with the vehicle closed up. A thinner
 walled budget box of the same volume can be half again as thirsty in the same conditions, which
 is why insulation quality is a battery sizing decision rather than a comfort one. The
 12V fridge roundup explains which units earn the premium
 and which ones quietly cost you a second battery.
Two habits cut the number materially. Park the fridge out of direct sun and give it air on all
 sides, because a compressor venting into a sealed cabinet works against itself. And pre-cool the
 contents before the trip, since pulling warm groceries down to temperature on day one is often
 the single biggest draw of the whole weekend.
 When does a station stop making sense and a DIY bank start?
The crossover is not about capacity, it is about charging. A station charges from a vehicle at
 roughly 100 to 400 watts depending on the input it offers. A wired DC-DC charger feeding a
 lithium house battery charges at 600 watts and up, which turns a two hour drive into a full
 refill. Once your travel pattern involves daily driving and daily heavy use, the wired system
 wins by a distance that no amount of extra station capacity closes.
Cost per usable amp-hour also flips. Two kilowatt-hours of station sits near under $1,000, while a
 200Ah lithium bank plus a charger and an inverter delivers more usable energy for a similar
 total and can be repaired component by component. What you pay for in the DIY version is your
 own labour, a real fusing plan and the risk that comes with both. The
 power station versus DIY battery bank 
comparison walks the whole decision end to end.
 Who should not buy the expert tier?
Do not buy the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 at
under $5,000 unless you have already measured a daily load that a 2kWh unit cannot cover. It
 weighs 113.5 lb, which makes it a payload decision before it is a power decision:
 that is most of the remaining margin on a loaded mid-size SUV once you have added a rooftop
 tent, water and recovery gear. Run the numbers through the
 payload weight calculator before you order,
 not after.
Do not agonise between the EcoFlow Delta 3 Max at
under $1,000 and the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 at
under $1,000, because they are the same 2kWh class within about one percent of capacity and
 within a few cents per watt-hour of each other. The Max adds faster AC recharging, about
1 hour from a wall outlet by the maker's figure, and that is exactly the
 thing you will not have on the trips this site is about. The Elite adds
200W more inverter and weighs
1.5 lb less. Buy the Max if you already own
 EcoFlow panels or routinely turn around at home mid-week. Otherwise the Elite is the pick.
And do not buy any 2kWh unit as a first purchase if your camping is currently one or two nights
 at a time. A under $500 station that gets used every weekend is a better outcome than a
under $1,000 station that stays in the garage because it is too heavy to bother lifting.
 Capacity you never discharge is money parked, and lithium ages on the shelf as well as in use.
 What do people get wrong when they buy one?
 Reading peak inverter watts as continuous watts. A 1800W station will surge higher for a second or two, and that surge figure is not a licence to run a 1800W kettle for ten minutes.
 Ignoring the solar input ceiling. Buying 600W of panels for a station that accepts 200W wastes two thirds of the array and all of the money.
 Charging from the cigarette socket and calling solar a failure. The socket is the bottleneck, not the panels.
 Forgetting the standby draw. Leaving the AC inverter switched on with nothing plugged in quietly costs 10 to 20 watts continuously, which is 240 to 480 watt-hours a day, or roughly half a small station.
 Storing it fully charged in a hot vehicle. Lithium keeps best around half charge in a cool place, and the difference over several years is real.
 Skipping the weight check. Everything in the expert tier is 50 lb or more, and roof and payload limits are unforgiving.
If this is your first electrical purchase for a vehicle, start at the
 overland power for beginners guide , which
 lays out the whole decision in order: load first, storage second, charging third, and hardware
 last. The station is the answer to two of those four questions at once, which is exactly why it
 is such a good first purchase and such a poor last one.
Want a smaller unit for a fridge-only setup? See the specs for the
 Dometic PLB15 and the
 Dometic PLB40 , and the
 van electrical system guide for how a station fits into a full build.
 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best portable power station for a vehicle build? For most vehicle builds the pick in this guide is the Bluetti Elite 200 V2: 2,073Wh of LiFePO4 capacity and a 2,600W inverter, roughly 162 amp-hours at 12.8V, enough to run a 45 quart fridge for about four days with no charging. Smaller and larger units are compared in the tiers above, ranked by watt-hours, inverter output and recharge speed. This is a researched comparison, not a lab review.
 What size portable power station do I need for a 12V fridge? A 45 quart compressor fridge draws roughly 30 to 45 amp-hours a day at 90F ambient, which is about 400 to 550 watt-hours. A 1kWh station such as the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at under $500 therefore runs a fridge for about 2.1 days with nothing else plugged in, and about a day and a half once you add lights and phone charging. A 2kWh station such as the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 at under $1,000 roughly doubles that to 4.1 days. Anything under 500Wh is a one-night unit.
 Can a portable power station replace a proper house battery? For weekend use, yes. A station is a battery, an inverter, a charge controller and a fuse block in one case, already assembled and already certified. What it cannot do is charge at high current from the alternator, hide under a bed, or scale past its own expansion limit. Full-time builds usually outgrow one, which is why the expandable models hold their value better than the sealed ones.
 How long does it take to recharge a power station while driving? From a 12V cigarette socket, very slowly. Most sockets are fused at 10 to 15A, which caps you near 120 to 180 watts, so a 1kWh station needs six to eight hours of driving. A dedicated wired 12V input at 8A or better, or a DC-DC charger feeding an Anderson connector, moves that to roughly two or three hours. Solar at 200W adds around 750 watt-hours on a clear day.
 Is LiFePO4 worth paying more for in a power station? Yes, and every station on this page uses it. LiFePO4 tolerates the shallow partial cycling a vehicle build inflicts on a battery every single day, and rated cycle life is typically 3,000 to 4,000 cycles against 500 or so for the older NMC packs. It is also far more tolerant of heat, which matters when the station lives in a closed vehicle parked in the sun.
 Can I use a power station below freezing? You can discharge one below freezing, but LiFePO4 cannot safely accept charge below 32F without internal heating. Most stations refuse to charge when the pack is cold and simply show an error, which reads like a fault and is actually the battery management system doing its job. Bring the unit inside the cab or the tent overnight and it will charge normally once the cells are above freezing.
 Do I need a 2000Wh station or will 1000Wh do? One kilowatt-hour covers a fridge, lights, a laptop and phone charging for two days, and it recharges from a 200W array in about a day and a half of good sun. Two kilowatt-hours is the point where you can stop rationing and run a coffee grinder or an induction burner briefly. Buy 1kWh if you drive most days and 2kWh if you sit still for three or four.
 How we choose: we compare published
 manufacturer specifications, standards documents including ABYC E-11, and verified owner
 reviews. We do not test gear in person. Vehicle payload, roof load and charging limits vary by
 model and year, so confirm yours against the door jamb sticker and the owner's manual rather
 than any number published here.

 Why RVs Need a Different Power Station Than Camping or Home Backup
 An RV is not a tent and it is not a house. It already has a converter, a house battery, and often shore power and generator hookups, so a portable power station is not your only power source — it is a supplement that fills specific gaps: quiet overnight power without running the generator, backup when the house battery is depleted, or a dedicated circuit for a CPAP, laptop, or mini-fridge that you do not want tied to the rig's main electrical system. That changes the buying calculus. You need enough continuous wattage to run real RV loads (a residential fridge draws 100-200W continuous with 1000W+ startup surge, a window AC draws 900-1500W), enough capacity to bridge a night or two without shore power, fast solar or AC recharging so you are not waiting all day, and a form factor that survives vibration, dust, and temperature swings on the road.

The standout for RV use specifically is the 1200W AC charge input and quiet 25dB operation — you can top it off from a campground pedestal in about an hour without it sounding like a box fan next to your bed.
 Trade-offs: at $1,299 it is the most expensive station on this list, and nearly 50 lb is a lot to move if you need to relocate it between the rig and a campsite.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 price on Amazon 
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2: Best Value for the Capacity
 The Explorer 2000 v2 gets you into the same 2kWh capacity tier as the C2000 Gen 2 for $300 less. Jackery's brand recognition and wide accessory ecosystem (solar panels, transfer switches, expansion batteries) make it an easy default if this is your first large power station and you want parts to be easy to find later. The 4400W surge ceiling is actually higher than the Anker's, which matters if you are running something with a hard motor-start spike, like a rooftop AC compressor or a residential fridge compressor kicking on.
 Trade-offs: at 43.5 lb it is only marginally lighter than the C2000 Gen 2, the AC recharge is slower (1100W vs 1200W input, and a less refined charge curve), and it lacks the C2000's ultra-quiet fan profile.
 Check the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 price on Amazon 
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: Best for Weekend Trips and Mid-Size Trailers
 Not everyone needs 2kWh. If your RV use is weekends and week-long trips rather than full-time boondocking, the C1000 Gen 2's 1024Wh capacity and 2000W inverter cover the essentials — lighting, device charging, a CPAP overnight, a coffee maker in the morning — without the size, weight, or price of the 2kWh-class units. Its class-leading 49-minute AC recharge means you can top it off during a lunch stop at a campground with shore power and be back to full before you leave.
 Trade-offs: 1024Wh will not carry a residential fridge or a window AC for long, and it has no solar input spec published at the same level as the larger C2000 Gen 2, so treat it as an AC-recharge-first unit.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 price on Amazon 
 Anker SOLIX C300: Best Compact Backup for Truck Campers
 For truck campers, teardrops, and anyone who just wants a dedicated power source for phones, a laptop, and a CPAP rather than running the whole rig, the C300's 288Wh pack is enough for 4-5 laptop charges or 4-6 hours of CPAP use. Its 140W USB-C PD port is the fastest laptop charging of any station on this list relative to its size, and at under 8 lb it is the only one you would comfortably hand-carry to a picnic table.
 Trade-offs: 288Wh will not touch fridge or AC loads, and there is no meaningful continuous AC wattage for larger appliances — this is a device-charging and small-load unit, not a house-power replacement.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C300 price on Amazon 
 How Much Power Station Capacity Does an RV Actually Need?
 Start with what you are trying to power and for how long, not the biggest number you can afford. A 12V compressor fridge draws roughly 40-60Wh per hour of runtime (it cycles, so real draw is lower than its rated wattage), which is about 1000-1400Wh over 24 hours — within reach of a single 2kWh station if it is your only load. A residential-style AC fridge draws more, closer to 1500-2500Wh per day. A window or mini-split AC unit is the real capacity killer: even a small 5,000 BTU unit can pull 400-600W continuous, which will drain a 2kWh station in under four hours of straight running, so AC use should be treated as a generator or shore-power task, not a power-station task, unless you are running one of the very large stations built for it. For most RVers, sizing to cover lighting, device charging, a fridge, and occasional small appliances for 1-2 days without recharge — call it 1,500-2,500Wh of usable capacity — hits the sweet spot. Use our power station wattage calculator to size your specific load list before buying.
 Solar Charging on the Road
 Solar is what makes a power station genuinely useful for extended RV travel instead of just glorified shore-power storage. The C2000 Gen 2 and Explorer 2000 v2 both accept up to 800W of solar input, which under good sun can recharge a depleted 2kWh unit in 2-3 hours — fast enough to fully reset overnight usage before you break camp. Portable panels are easier for RVers than roof-mounted ones because you can angle them toward the sun and move them into shade-free spots at each new site, rather than being stuck with whatever angle your roof happens to face. See our guide on choosing solar panels for a power station for panel wattage and connector compatibility.
 RV-Specific Connections: Shore Power, 30A, and Transfer Switches
 If you want a power station to feed part of your RV's existing wiring rather than just running loose extension cords to individual appliances, you need to think about how it connects. Most portable power stations output standard NEMA 5-15 household outlets, not the 30A or 50A shore-power plugs RVs use, so you will need an adapter or a properly installed transfer switch to route power into your rig's breaker panel safely — never back-feed a panel without a transfer switch. Our guide on connecting a power station to an RV 30A outlet covers the adapter path, and understanding NEMA TT-30 and RV adapter compatibility explains which adapter matches which rig. For a broader look at built-in RV integration features across brands, see our roundup of power stations with the best RV and camper integration .
 Common Mistakes RVers Make When Choosing a Power Station
 The most common error is buying based on capacity alone and ignoring continuous wattage — a 2kWh station with only a 1000W inverter cannot run a microwave or a hair dryer even though it has plenty of stored energy. The second is skipping solar input specs entirely: a station that only recharges from AC shore power is far less useful once you are boondocking for more than a night. The third is buying a unit too heavy to move between the rig and a campsite when you actually wanted portability, or conversely buying a lightweight small-capacity unit and expecting it to run a fridge for days. Match the unit to your actual trip style — weekend camper, full-time boondocker, or backup-only — rather than the biggest sale price you see.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a portable power station run my RV air conditioner? Only briefly, and only the largest stations. A small 5,000 BTU unit needs 400-600W continuous with a startup surge that can spike past 1500W, which will drain even a 2kWh station in a few hours. For sustained AC use, plan on shore power or a generator, and treat a power station as backup for everything else.
 What size power station do I need for a weekend RV trip? For lighting, device charging, and a CPAP or small fridge over a weekend without recharging, 1,000-1,500Wh of capacity with at least a 1500W inverter is usually enough. Use our wattage calculator to total your specific appliance list before deciding.
 Is it safe to wire a power station into my RVs electrical panel? Only with a properly installed transfer switch that prevents the power station and shore power or generator from being connected simultaneously. Running loose extension cords to individual appliances is simpler and safer for most RVers than panel integration.
 How long does it take to recharge a power station with RV solar? A 2kWh-class station with 800W of solar input can recharge from empty in roughly 2-3 hours under strong, direct sun, though cloud cover, panel angle, and shading from trees at a campsite will meaningfully slow that down.
 Should I buy one large power station or two smaller ones for an RV? One large station is simpler to manage and charges faster overall, but two smaller units let you run one at the rig while carrying the other to a picnic table or tent site, and give you redundancy if one fails mid-trip. Full-time RVers often prefer one large unit; occasional campers benefit more from a mid-size unit plus a compact backup like the SOLIX C300.

results.snippet: The Anker Solix S2000 is a 2,000Wh portable power station with a 1,500W continuous AC output, four UK Type G sockets, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a five-year warranty. Its upright, compact design and front-and-rear socket layout suit home backup and DIY use, though at 16.2kg it is not light to carry, and both sides need access to use all outlets. In a practical test, it powered repeated sessions with a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum over a seven-hour workday, starting at 59% charge and ending at 13%; this was intermittent use, not a controlled capacity test. Mains charging reached roughly 1,070W in observed snapshots, while solar input is limited to 400W. The clear display and straightforward app provide useful monitoring and controls, including charging limits, schedules, and UPS modes. Anker rates UPS transfer at about 10ms, but this was not independently tested. The main caveat is the output ceiling: check appliance ratings and starting demands, as the large battery cannot run every high-wattage appliance.

 The Anker Solix S2000 made a strong first impression by being useful immediately. Starting at 59%, it covered my intermittent vacuum use throughout a working day and finished with charge remaining.
Its biggest strengths are that useful battery capacity, sensible socket layout and an app that makes the controls understandable. The output ceiling needs consideration, but for compatible equipment, DIY jobs and household backup, there’s plenty to like.

 Portable power stations are useful for everything from keeping your broadband running during a power cut to powering equipment away from a convenient socket. The Anker Solix S2000 fits both roles, combining a substantial battery with a relatively compact upright design.
 What impressed me most, though, was how little fuss it involved. It handled repeated sessions with a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum straight out of the box, while the accompanying app was easy to set up and refreshingly clear about what its settings actually do.

 Design and connections 
 The S2000 has an understated appearance: a dark grey enclosure, rounded edges and a glossy front panel. It looks perfectly at home beside a desk, although mine was soon earning its keep around DIY equipment.
 Its upright shape gives it a reasonably small footprint. At 16.2kg, however, “portable” still involves a deliberate lift. Moving it between rooms or taking it out to the garden is one thing; carrying it a long distance is another.
 The UK version has four proper Type G sockets, split evenly between the front and rear. That arrangement makes sense. You can keep regularly connected equipment plugged in behind the unit, leaving the front sockets available for things you connect occasionally.
 There is a trade-off: you’ll need access to both sides if you want to use every socket. Bear that in mind before squeezing it into a tight space, and leave the ventilation clear.

 The USB connections sit above the display. The 100W USB-C port is the one to choose for a compatible laptop, while the other USB-C connection is limited to 15W. They look similar, so it’s worth checking the labels.
 The screen puts the remaining battery percentage front and centre, alongside input and output wattage and an estimated remaining time. That gives you the information you need without reaching for your phone.
 Performance: a proper day’s work 
 My S2000 arrived with a 59% state of charge. Rather than charging it fully before doing anything useful, I put it straight to work powering a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum.
 Between approximately 10am and 5pm, I used the vacuum repeatedly in sessions lasting around five to ten minutes. The Anker handled those sessions without any problems, and by the time I finished, it still showed 13% remaining.
 To be clear, that was intermittent use across a seven-hour working day, rather than seven hours of continuous vacuuming. Even so, it was a useful practical test: repeated use of a fairly demanding appliance, starting with little more than half a battery.
 The benefit was simple. I could get on with the job without running an extension lead back to a mains socket, and the power station had enough charge to cover the work I needed to do.
 This wasn’t a controlled capacity test. I didn’t record the vacuum’s total running time or measure the energy delivered at the socket, so it wouldn’t be fair to calculate an efficiency figure from the percentage drop.
 What I can say is that it coped comfortably with this particular vacuum and pattern of use.
 The main limitation is the 1,500W continuous output. Battery capacity tells you how much energy is stored; output determines which appliances it can run. A large battery doesn’t automatically mean it can power a typical high-wattage UK kettle or several demanding tools together.
 Check appliance ratings, allow for starting demands, and remember that the output limit is shared across the AC sockets.
 Charging options 
 (Image credit: Future) For everyday charging, the S2000 connects directly to the mains using the supplied AC cable. There’s no separate external power brick to find space for.
 During one charging session, the front display showed approximately 1,068W going in. An app screenshot taken during charging showed around 1,077W, with UltraFast charging switched off. These are snapshots rather than a timed charging test, but they show a substantial charging rate in normal use.
 There’s also an app-controlled UltraFast option when a quicker turnaround matters.
 Away from home, the S2000 supports compatible solar panels and vehicle charging, provided you have the correct cables and accessories. Solar input is capped at 400W, with Anker specifying a maximum open-circuit voltage of 60V. Panel compatibility matters as well as the connector.
 Those alternatives add flexibility, although a normal car accessory socket will be much slower than mains charging. Think of it as a way to replenish charge while travelling, rather than expecting a quick refill of a 2kWh battery.
 The app: easy to set up, easy to understand 
 (Image credit: Future || Anker) The app was one of the nicest surprises.
 Finding it in the Google Play Store was straightforward, as were signing in and getting started. The S2000 was detected straight away, added without difficulty and ready to control. An iPhone version also appears to be available, although my experience here was with Android.
 The main screen presents the battery percentage, temperature, charging estimate and power flow clearly. You can see what’s happening at a glance.
 More useful still is the depth of control. There are multiple UPS and power-management modes, charging timers, adjustable AC charging power and battery charge limits. You also get AC output scheduling, a countdown to switch the sockets off, screen controls and power-usage history.
 Crucially, the explanations are good. Rather than leaving you to decipher a vaguely named mode, the app helps you understand what a setting does and decide whether it suits your needs.
 Some power-station apps make configuration feel like educated guesswork. Here, the guidance makes the extra features more approachable, particularly if this is your first battery system.
 Backup power and everyday use 
 The UPS function adds another potential role: keeping suitable equipment powered when the mains fails. Anker quotes a transfer time of around 10ms, although I haven’t independently measured that or tested compatibility with individual computers.
 For a home office, the combination of rear sockets, battery monitoring and configurable operating modes is appealing. You can leave equipment connected and manage the unit without constantly handling it.

 This guide is for people who have already settled on a size bracket and are now choosing between units that look almost identical on a listing page. We compared four power stations with continuous inverter ratings from 2000W to 2400W, all of them LiFePO4, on the four things that actually separate them: surge headroom, watt-hours per pound, how much energy each one puts back per minute of charging, and how far the capacity can grow later. We did not test these units, and every review states exactly what its recommendation rests on. What you get here is the arithmetic a retailer listing leaves out, a clear explanation of why 2000W and 2000Wh are unrelated numbers, and the reason two of these four publish no surge rating at all.
 What is the best 2000W portable power station?
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 suits the most buyers in this bracket. It holds 2042Wh at 39.5 lb, which is 51.7 watt-hours per pound and the best carry ratio of the four, and its 2200W inverter leaves 700W spare above a 1500W appliance. If you need published surge headroom for a motor, the OUPES Mega 1 states 4500W where Jackery states nothing.
 Key takeaways
 2000W is an inverter rating and has nothing to do with how much energy the unit stores; watt-hours is the capacity number
 Model numbers lie in both directions in this bracket, so read the continuous inverter rating rather than the name on the case
 Watt-hours per pound ranges from 28.4 to 51.7 across these four units, which is a bigger practical gap than any capacity difference between them
 The fastest recharge on the clock is not the fastest recharge in watt-hours, because a smaller pack finishes sooner while moving less energy
 Two of these four publish no surge rating, so nobody can tell you what they do with a compressor or pump start
 Our picks at a glance
Every unit below wins a specific situation rather than a place in a ranking. Pick the row that
 matches how you will actually use it.

 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 
 People who move a full two kilowatt-hours between a garage, a truck bed and a campsite rather than leaving the unit parked in one room.

 The full reviews
 The Explorer 2000 v2 carries 2042Wh at 39.5 lb, which is 51.7 watt-hours for every pound you lift. Nothing else in this bracket comes close on that ratio, and the trade is a spec sheet with no published surge figure and a single USB port.
 + 
What we like
 about the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 
 2042Wh at 39.5 lb works out to 51.7Wh per pound, the best carry ratio of the four units here
 2200W across three AC ports leaves 700W spare while a 1500W appliance is running
 20ms UPS switchover is fast enough that a desktop or router does not reboot when the grid drops
 66 minutes to 80% restores roughly 1634Wh, so a single lunch break on the wall covers most of a night
 − 
Where it falls short
 for the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 
 Jackery publishes 2200W continuous but no surge rating at all, so there is no stated headroom for a compressor, pump or saw start
 One USB-C PD port is the entire USB provision on a 2kWh unit, so anything more than a laptop and a phone has to go through the AC outlets
 No expansion battery is listed, so 2042Wh is a permanent ceiling, while the BLUETTI AC200L in this guide reaches 8192Wh and the OUPES Mega 1 reaches 5120Wh
 Check price at 
 Key specifications
 Capacity 2042Wh 
 AC output 2200W across 3 AC ports 
 Weight 39.5 lb (17.9 kg) 
 AC recharge time 66 minutes to 80% 
 UPS switchover 20ms 
 Warranty 5 year manufacturer 
 The argument for this unit is a division sum. Divide 2042Wh by 39.5 lb and you get
51.7 watt-hours per pound. Do the same for the other three units in this guide and
you get 36.8, 33.4 and 28.4. In a bracket where every unit does roughly the same
job, that gap is the decision.
 What the weight actually buys back # 
 Weight in this category is not vanity. A 2000W-class unit that lives permanently in
a basement corner is a different purchase from one that goes in a vehicle every
other weekend. The second one gets used; the first one gets forgotten.
 At 39.5 lb the Explorer 2000 v2 is the only unit here carrying a full 2kWh that one
adult can realistically lift into a truck bed without planning the movement. The
BLUETTI AC200L holds six more watt-hours and weighs 21.9 lb more to do it.
 Runtime, with the assumption stated # 
 Rated capacity is not usable capacity. Inverter conversion costs you something, and
a reasonable working assumption is that around 85% of the rating reaches the outlet.
On that basis 2042Wh becomes roughly 1736Wh at the socket.
 Against a full-size refrigerator averaging 150W across its compressor duty cycle,
that is about 11.6 hours. Against an 1800W load with no cycling, it is about 58
minutes. Both numbers come from the same pack, which is why “how long does it last”
has no single answer until you name the load.
 A day of fridge duty is roughly 3.6kWh, so a full charge here covers a little under
half of one.
 The missing surge number # 
 The published figure is 2200W across three AC ports. There is no surge or peak
rating alongside it.
 That matters because motor loads do not draw their running wattage at start-up.
A compressor pulls several times its running draw for a fraction of a second, and
the specification that tells you whether the inverter rides that out is the surge
rating. The OUPES Mega 1 publishes 4500W. The Goal Zero Yeti 1500 publishes 3600W.
Jackery publishes nothing, and we are not going to guess on its behalf.
 For electronics, lighting, a fridge you have already confirmed starts on similar
hardware, or resistive loads like a kettle, this is not a problem. For a pump, a
compressor or a table saw, the absence of a number is itself the answer: choose a
unit that states one.
 One USB port # 
 Three AC outlets and one 100W USB-C is a thin port list for a pack this size. It is
a genuine limitation on a camping trip where four people arrive with phones. The
workaround is a multi-port charger in an AC outlet, which works fine and costs you
a little conversion efficiency, but it is an extra thing to remember to pack.
 2042Wh is the ceiling, not the starting point # 
 No expansion battery is listed for this unit, so the capacity you buy is the capacity
you keep. Two of the other three units here are not built that way: the BLUETTI AC200L
reaches 8192Wh and the OUPES Mega 1 reaches 5120Wh with two B2 batteries.
 That is fine if 2042Wh is genuinely enough, and it is the one constraint in this
bracket you cannot fix after the fact. If your power use is trending upwards, weigh
that against the carry ratio before the carry ratio decides it for you.
 Specification comparison 
How we evaluated this
 We did not test this unit. It was assessed by comparing published specifications against the units we have used.
 We did not run this unit. Placement is based on the published JE-2000D specifications, compared against the capacity, weight and inverter ratings of the other three units in this guide, with all runtime figures calculated from rated capacity and a stated conversion loss assumption.
 Sources
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 product specifications (manufacturer) 
 What this evaluation does not cover
 We have not measured usable capacity, which always falls below the 2042Wh rating
 The 66-minute recharge claim is unverified at low states of charge or in a warm room
 The 20ms UPS switchover figure has not been independently measured
 No surge rating is published, so we cannot say what this unit does with a motor start
 Best for People who move a full two kilowatt-hours between a garage, a truck bed and a campsite rather than leaving the unit parked in one room. 
 Choose something else if You want a published surge number before trusting a unit with a refrigerator compressor, a well pump or a large corded tool, or you expect to add battery capacity later, because no expansion battery is listed for this unit. 
 A 4500W surge on a 2000W inverter is a 2.25x margin, the widest published start-up headroom in this bracket, and it arrives in a 27.8 lb box. The catch is the pack behind it: 1024Wh is half what the other units here hold.
 + 
What we like
 about the OUPES Mega 1 
 4500W surge against a 2000W continuous rating is a 2.25x margin, the widest of the four units compared here
 27.8 lb is 11.7 lb lighter than the next unit and the only one here a single person carries one-handed
 36 minutes to 80% on AC, or 26 minutes with AC and solar together, is the fastest wall-clock refill in this guide
 Expands to 5120Wh with two B2 batteries, five times the base pack, so the small capacity is not permanent
 3,500+ rated cycles to 80% against 1024Wh is roughly 3,584kWh of lifetime throughput
 − 
Where it falls short
 for the OUPES Mega 1 
 1024Wh is half the capacity of every other 2000W-class unit here, so a 150W refrigerator gets about 5.8 hours rather than 11.6
 The 36-minute headline restores only about 819Wh, which is 22.8Wh per minute against the BLUETTI AC200L's 36.4, so it is the fastest clock and the slowest energy transfer
 Getting to a useful overnight capacity means buying two B2 expansion batteries, which turns the lightest unit here into a stack you no longer carry one-handed
 Check price at

 AC output 2000W (4500W surge) 
 Capacity 1024Wh 
 Weight 27.8 lb (12.6 kg) 
 AC recharge time 36 minutes to 80% on AC, 26 minutes with AC and solar together 
 UPS switchover Under 20ms 
 Expandable Yes, to 5120Wh with two B2 extra batteries 
 Rated cycle life 3,500+ cycles to 80% 
 Most units in this bracket are bought for capacity. This one is bought for the
moment the load switches on.
 Why the surge margin is the whole pitch # 
 Divide 4500 by 2000 and you get 2.25. That is the multiple by which this inverter
can exceed its continuous rating for a start-up transient. For comparison, the Goal
Zero Yeti 1500 publishes 3600W over 2000W, a 1.8x margin, and two units in this
guide publish no surge figure whatsoever.
 That matters because motors do not draw their running wattage when they start. A
compressor, a well pump, a shop vac or a mitre saw pulls a brief multiple of its
running draw, and an inverter without margin trips rather than starts. A unit that
cannot start a load cannot run it, no matter how many watt-hours sit behind it.
 What is not published is how long that 4500W is held. A surge figure without a
duration is half a specification, and we are treating it as such.
 The capacity is the price you pay # 
 1024Wh is not a 2kWh pack. Applying the same 85% conversion assumption we use
throughout this guide gives roughly 870Wh at the outlet.
 Against a refrigerator averaging 150W across its duty cycle, that is about 5.8
hours. Against a 1500W circular saw drawing continuously, it is around 35 minutes,
although a saw cuts in bursts so real working time is far longer than that figure
suggests. Against a full day of fridge duty, which is roughly 3.6kWh, one charge
covers about a quarter.
 For a workshop this is usually fine, because tool use is intermittent and the wall
is nearby. For an overnight outage it is not, and that is the line to check yourself
against before buying.
 The recharge figure is smaller than it looks # 
 Thirty-six minutes to 80% is the fastest number in this guide, and it is genuinely
useful when you are working near a socket. But 80% of 1024Wh is about 819Wh, which
means 22.8Wh restored for every minute plugged in.
 The BLUETTI AC200L takes 45 minutes, nine minutes longer, and restores about
1638Wh in that time, or 36.4Wh per minute. If your constraint is a short window at
a socket, the OUPES wins. If your constraint is total energy back in the pack, it
does not. Both statements come from the same two specifications.
 Expansion changes the unit # 
 Two B2 batteries take it to 5120Wh, five times the base pack and the largest
multiple on this shortlist. That is a real answer to the capacity problem.
 It is also the end of the 27.8 lb argument. Once you are hauling a stack, the
reason you chose this unit over the Jackery has gone, and you should compare the
expanded system against the BLUETTI AC200L’s 8192Wh ceiling instead.
 Specification comparison 
How we evaluated this
 We did not test this unit. It was assessed by comparing published specifications against the units we have used.
 We have not powered a tool from this unit. The assessment compares the published S1 specifications against the other three units in this guide, with the surge margin, watt-hours per pound and recharge throughput figures calculated from those published numbers rather than measured.
 Sources
 OUPES Mega 1 product specifications (manufacturer) 
 What this evaluation does not cover
 The 4500W surge has not been verified against any specific motor or compressor
 Surge duration is not published, so we cannot say how long that margin is held
 Usable capacity below the 1024Wh rating has not been measured
 Expansion behaviour with B2 batteries attached, including recharge time, is untested
 Best for Job sites, workshops and garages where the hard part is starting a compressor, pump or saw rather than running anything for hours on end. 
 Choose something else if You need the base unit alone to cover an overnight outage, because 1024Wh does not stretch across a night once a refrigerator and lighting are on it. 
 The AC200L is the one unit here that plugs a trailer in directly through a 30A RV port and grows to 8192Wh afterwards. It also weighs 61.41 lb, so the sensible purchase is the one where it gets installed somewhere and stays put.
 + 
What we like
 about the BLUETTI AC200L 
 A built-in 30A RV port feeds a trailer directly rather than through an adapter chain
 45 minutes to 80% restores roughly 1638Wh, about 36.4Wh for every minute plugged in, the highest energy transfer rate here
 A 1200W solar input ceiling is high enough to move a meaningful share of a 2048Wh pack in a day even at the fraction of rated output real panels deliver
 Expands to 8192Wh, four times the base capacity and the largest ceiling on this shortlist
 2400W continuous leaves 900W spare while a 1500W appliance is already running
 − 
Where it falls short
 for the BLUETTI AC200L 
 61.41 lb for 2048Wh works out to 33.4Wh per pound, against 51.7 for the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, which holds effectively the same capacity and weighs 21.9 lb less
 The 2400W rating is published with no surge figure, so there is no stated margin for a compressor or pump start
 At 16.5 x 11 x 14.4 in it occupies floor space rather than shelf space, which is a real constraint in a van conversion

 Max solar input 1200W 
 Expandable Yes, to 8192Wh with expansion batteries 
 Ports 11 ports, including a 30A RV port and a 48V/8A DC port 
 Weight 61.41 lb (27.9 kg) 
 Two of the four units in this guide hold roughly 2048Wh. One of them weighs 39.5 lb
and one weighs 61.41 lb. If capacity were the only thing that mattered, the AC200L
would have nothing to say. It has two things.
 The 30A RV port # 
 This is the feature that puts the AC200L in a category of one on this shortlist.
A travel trailer’s shore power cord goes straight in. No adapter chain, no
splitting the load across household outlets, no guessing whether the pigtail you
bought is rated for the draw.
 For anyone powering a trailer, that single port is worth more than the 22 lb weight
penalty, because the unit lives in a bay or a cabinet and never gets carried
anywhere. The weight only becomes a problem for buyers who intended to move it.
 Energy back per minute, not minutes on the clock # 
 The published recharge is 0 to 80% in 45 minutes at 2400W AC input. Eighty percent
of 2048Wh is about 1638Wh, so that is roughly 36.4Wh restored for every minute
plugged in.
 Run the same arithmetic on the others and the ranking changes. The OUPES Mega 1
finishes in 36 minutes but moves about 819Wh, or 22.8Wh per minute. The Jackery
takes 66 minutes for about 1634Wh, or 24.8Wh per minute. The AC200L is not the
fastest to reach a full bar; it is by a clear margin the fastest at putting energy
back, which is what matters when the grid is intermittent or the generator only
runs for an hour.
 Solar, honestly # 
 1200W is the rated input ceiling. Panels almost never hit their rating, so treat
that number as a limit rather than a forecast: angle, cloud, temperature and cable
losses all take a share. Even at a conservative fraction of the ceiling, though,
this is enough input to move a meaningful part of a 2048Wh pack inside one day,
which is not true of units with a 400W or 500W ceiling.
 The expansion ceiling, and the honest caveat # 
 8192Wh is four times the base pack, the largest ceiling of the four units here.
That makes the AC200L a reasonable first purchase for someone who expects their
power use to grow, because the ceiling is high enough that the base unit is unlikely
to become the bottleneck.
 The caveat is that expansion batteries are additional purchases, and we cannot tell
you how recharge time behaves with them attached because that figure is not
published. Buy the base unit for what it does today, and treat the ceiling as
insurance rather than a plan.
 Research based 
How we evaluated this

 Despite the 1500 on the case this is a 2000W inverter with a 3600W surge, and its real advantage is the port panel: four AC outlets and six USB including a 140W USB-C.  Rated cycle life 4,000 cycles 
 Weight 52.9 lb (24.0 kg) 
 AC recharge time Under 1 hour from 0% to 80% from the wall 
 The name is misleading in the buyer’s favour for once. A Yeti 1500 in this
generation carries a 2000W inverter with a 3600W surge, which puts it squarely in
this bracket even though the number on the case suggests otherwise.
 The port panel is the reason to buy it # 
 Four AC outlets, six USB ports including a 140W USB-C, a 12V vehicle outlet, an HPP
output and two 6mm outlets. That is fourteen sockets. The closest of the other three
is the BLUETTI AC200L at a published eleven, and it reaches that count partly through
a 30A RV port and a 48V DC port rather than through outlets a phone or a laptop can
use.
 That sounds like a minor convenience until you are the person running a market
stall, a photo booth, a repair bench or a classroom cart. The alternative is a
power strip in one AC outlet, which works, but it means every device is passing
through an extra conversion and an extra thing to trip over. The 140W USB-C in
particular runs a large laptop directly off DC without an inverter in the path at
all, which is quietly more efficient than plugging its brick into an AC socket.
 What it costs you in capacity # 
 1505Wh at 52.9 lb is 28.4 watt-hours per pound. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is
51.7. In plain terms: this unit weighs 13.4 lb more than the Jackery and holds
537Wh less.
 At the 85% conversion assumption we apply across this guide, 1505Wh is about 1279Wh
at the outlet. That is roughly 8.5 hours of a 150W refrigerator, or about 43 minutes
of an 1800W continuous draw, or a bit over a third of a 3.6kWh fridge day.
 Those are respectable numbers. They are just not 2kWh numbers, and buyers comparing
this against the AC200L or the Jackery on capacity alone will not see that until
they check the spec.
 Cycle life is the long game # 
 4,000 rated cycles multiplied by 1505Wh is roughly 6,020kWh of energy through the
pack over its rated life. The OUPES Mega 1’s 3,500 cycles against 1024Wh gives about
3,584kWh. The other two units here do not publish a cycle figure, so they cannot be
placed on that scale.
 If this unit is going to be cycled daily on a bench rather than sitting charged
waiting for an outage, that throughput number is the specification that matters
most, and it is the one this unit leads on.
 The gap in the sheet # 
 There is no published UPS switchover time. For a bench full of phones and tools
that is irrelevant, because none of those loads care about a brief interruption.
For a desktop, a NAS or a network rack it is decisive, and the absence of a figure
means you should assume it is not the job this unit was built for.
 Specification comparison 
How we evaluated this
 We did not test this unit. It was assessed by comparing published specifications against the units we have used.
 We did not use this unit. Placement is based on Goal Zero's published 6th generation Yeti 1500 specifications, compared on inverter rating, port count, capacity and weight against the other three units here. Lifetime throughput is calculated by multiplying rated cycle life by rated capacity.
 Sources
 Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th Gen) product specifications (manufacturer) 
 What this evaluation does not cover
 We have not measured simultaneous draw across the AC and USB ports
 The 4,000 cycle rating is a manufacturer figure and reflects a lab duty cycle, not household use
 Usable capacity below the 1505Wh rating has not been measured
 No UPS switchover figure is published, so we cannot assess its behaviour during a grid cut
 Best for Workbenches, editing desks, craft rooms and market stalls where a dozen things need charging at once and the unit is not going anywhere. 
 Choose something else if You are choosing on watt-hours per pound, or you expect to add battery capacity later, because neither is a strength of this unit. 
 How we researched this guide
 Four units with continuous inverter ratings between 2000W and 2400W were compared using published manufacturer specifications, with aggregated owner reports drawn on only where an individual review names them as a source. None were tested by us. Every runtime figure in this guide is calculated from rated capacity assuming roughly 85% reaches the outlet after conversion loss, and every review states which sources its recommendation rests on.
The full process is on our how we test portable power stations page,
 including what counts as hands-on use.
 Units evaluated 4 
 Used hands-on 0 
 Assessed from documentation and owner reports 4 
 Evaluation methods used: specification comparison, documentation and owner-report research 
 What to look for before you buy
 2000W and 2000Wh are unrelated numbers # 
 Almost every confused purchase in this bracket starts here.
 Watts describe rate. A 2000W inverter can deliver 2000 watts at any given instant,
and that is what decides whether an appliance will run at all. Watt-hours describe
quantity. A 2048Wh pack holds 2048 watt-hours of energy, and that is what decides
how long it runs for.
 The two are set independently. The OUPES Mega 1 in this guide is rated 2000W and
holds 1024Wh. The BLUETTI AC200L is rated 2400W and holds 2048Wh, exactly double the
storage for a 20% higher inverter rating. Both are correctly described as 2000W-class
units, and they answer completely different questions.
 If you are shopping this bracket, decide which number you were actually searching
for before you compare anything else.
 The name on the case is not the inverter rating # 
 The model number is not a specification and cannot be trusted in either direction.
 The Goal Zero Yeti 1500 in this guide carries a 2000W inverter with a 3600W surge,
so it belongs in this bracket despite the number on the case. Meanwhile the Anker
SOLIX S2000, which most people would assume is a 2000W unit, is rated 1500W
continuous. Two units, two misleading names, in opposite directions.
 Read the continuous AC output figure on the specification sheet. Nothing in the
model designation or the marketing copy around it is load-bearing.
 Watt-hours per pound separates these four more than capacity does # 
 Three of these four units hold between 1505Wh and 2048Wh. On paper that is a narrow
band. Divide by weight and the band opens up:
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2: 2042Wh at 39.5 lb, 51.7Wh per pound
 OUPES Mega 1: 1024Wh at 27.8 lb, 36.8Wh per pound
 BLUETTI AC200L: 2048Wh at 61.41 lb, 33.4Wh per pound
 Goal Zero Yeti 1500: 1505Wh at 52.9 lb, 28.4Wh per pound
 The extreme case is worth sitting with. The Jackery and the AC200L hold effectively
the same energy, within six watt-hours of each other, and one of them weighs 21.9 lb
more to do it. If the unit is being installed in a trailer bay, that is irrelevant
and the AC200L’s RV port and expansion ceiling win. If it is going in and out of a
vehicle, it is the whole decision.
 Runtime, with the assumption written down # 
 Manufacturer runtime charts assume a constant, convenient draw. Here is the
arithmetic instead, with the assumption stated: rated capacity is not what reaches
the outlet, and around 85% after conversion loss is a reasonable working figure.
 Against a full-size refrigerator averaging 150W across its compressor duty cycle:
 2042Wh Jackery: about 11.6 hours
 2048Wh AC200L: about 11.6 hours
 1505Wh Yeti 1500: about 8.5 hours
 1024Wh OUPES: about 5.8 hours
 Against an 1800W continuous load with no cycling, the same packs give roughly 58,
58, 43 and 29 minutes. A day of fridge duty is around 3.6kWh, so even the largest
unit here covers a little under half of one. That is the honest ceiling of this
bracket, and anyone planning for multi-day coverage needs solar input or expansion
batteries rather than a bigger single unit.
 Surge ratings, and the two that do not have one # 
 A motor does not draw its running wattage when it starts. A compressor, a pump or a
saw pulls a brief multiple of that figure, and the surge rating is the specification
telling you whether the inverter rides it out.
 OUPES publishes 4500W over a 2000W continuous rating, a 2.25x margin. Goal Zero
publishes 3600W over 2000W, 1.8x. Jackery publishes 2200W across three AC ports with
no surge figure, and BLUETTI publishes 2400W with no surge figure.
 That absence is not proof of a weak inverter, but it does mean nobody can tell you
what those two do with a motor start. For electronics, lighting and resistive loads
it changes nothing. For a pump, a compressor or a large tool, buy the unit that
states a number.
 Recharge speed: clock time versus watt-hours returned # 
 The headline figure everyone quotes is minutes to 80%. It is the wrong figure on its
own, because a smaller pack reaches 80% sooner while moving less energy.
 Convert to watt-hours restored per minute plugged in:
 BLUETTI AC200L: about 1638Wh in 45 minutes, 36.4Wh per minute
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2: about 1634Wh in 66 minutes, 24.8Wh per minute
 OUPES Mega 1: about 819Wh in 36 minutes, 22.8Wh per minute
 Goal Zero Yeti 1500: about 1204Wh in under an hour, at least 20.1Wh per minute
 The OUPES has the fastest clock and the slowest energy transfer. Both facts come
from the same two specifications, and which one matters depends on whether your
constraint is a short window at a socket or the total energy back in the pack.
 Growing past 2kWh # 
 Two of these four expand. The AC200L reaches 8192Wh, four times its base pack and
the highest ceiling here. The OUPES Mega 1 reaches 5120Wh with two B2 batteries,
which is a five-fold multiple of a much smaller start.
 The Jackery and the Yeti 1500 do not list expansion, so their rated capacity is
permanent. That is fine if it is enough, and it is a real constraint if your power
use is heading upwards. Decide which of those is true before you buy, because it is
the one thing in this bracket you cannot fix later.
 Which one should you buy?
Match your situation on the left to the recommendation on the right.
 You will carry the unit between a house, a vehicle and a campsite
 Recommendation: Buy the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, at 51.7Wh per pound the best carry ratio here 
 You need to start a compressor, pump or large corded tool
 Recommendation: Buy the OUPES Mega 1, the only unit here publishing a 4500W surge on a 2000W inverter 
 You are powering a travel trailer through its shore power cord
 Recommendation: Buy the BLUETTI AC200L for its built-in 30A RV port 
 You expect your power needs to grow well past 2kWh
 Recommendation: Buy the BLUETTI AC200L, which expands to 8192Wh, four times its base pack 
 You need many devices charging at once from a unit that stays put
 Recommendation: Buy the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 for its four AC outlets and six USB ports 
 You need the unit to hold up a desktop or a NAS through a grid cut
 Recommendation: Buy the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 or OUPES Mega 1, the only two here publishing a 20ms or faster switchover 
 Mistakes buyers make
 Reading the 2000W inverter rating as 2000 watt-hours of storage and buying a unit with half the capacity expected
 Trusting a model number, because a unit branded 2000 can carry a 1500W inverter and one branded 1500 can carry a 2000W one
 Comparing two units whose capacities sit within six watt-hours of each other and missing that one of them weighs 21.9 lb more
 Buying a unit with no published surge rating for a refrigerator, pump or power tool that has to start against a compressor
 Choosing on the headline recharge time rather than on how many watt-hours actually go back into the pack in that time
 Assuming a rated solar input is what panels will deliver, when angle, cloud and cable losses all take a share
 Our final recommendation
If you want one answer rather than a shortlist, this is the unit that suits the widest
 range of readers in this category.
 Best for moving 2kWh on your own 
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 
 People who move a full two kilowatt-hours between a garage, a truck bed and a campsite rather than leaving the unit parked in one room.

 Questions buyers ask
 Does a 2000W power station store 2000 watt-hours?
 No, and this is the single most common mistake in this bracket. Watts describe how much the inverter can deliver at any instant. Watt-hours describe how much energy is stored. The OUPES Mega 1 here is rated 2000W and holds 1024Wh, so it can deliver a large load but not for very long.
 Can a 2000W power station run a refrigerator?
 A 2000W continuous rating is comfortably above what a household fridge draws while running. The question is whether the inverter survives the compressor start, which draws a brief multiple of the running figure. Check the surge rating rather than the continuous one, and be cautious with any unit that does not publish a surge number.
 Can it run a window air conditioner?
 A small window unit is usually within a 2000W continuous rating, but air conditioners start against a compressor in the same way a fridge does, and they run for hours rather than cycling briefly. Capacity becomes the limit long before the inverter does, so size on watt-hours and expect a fraction of a night rather than a full one.
 How much do these weigh and can one person move them?
 The four here range from 27.8 lb to 61.41 lb. Anything under about 40 lb is a realistic single-person carry over a short distance. The BLUETTI AC200L at 61.41 lb is a two-person lift on stairs or into a tailgate, which is why it suits an installation rather than a unit you move around.
 Is LiFePO4 worth insisting on at this size?
 Yes. Every unit in this guide uses it, and the reason is cycle life. Goal Zero rates the Yeti 1500 at 4,000 cycles and OUPES rates the Mega 1 at over 3,500 to 80% capacity. At a size where the unit is a long-term purchase, a chemistry that survives daily cycling for years is the difference between one purchase and two.
